inflation_management: The Cook Islands are self-governing in free association with New Zealand and use the New Zealand dollar, so they import New Zealand monetary policy and have no IMF data series. Tourism - the dominant sector - makes prices and activity highly cyclical: the 2008-09 downturn, then the COVID border closure, produced deflationary collapses in activity, while reopening brought sharp rebounds. Inflation management is not a domestic policy question; tourism demand is.
debt_management: The government borrows modestly, mostly on concessional terms, and ran a strong fiscal position before COVID on tourism receipts. The pandemic's tourism wipeout forced borrowing that lifted debt sharply, but the 2022-23 reopening restored revenues fast. The structural fiscal question is the same as ever: a tourism monoculture means the budget has no shock absorber except reserves and donor support.

key_events.event: February: Cyclone Pat devastated Aitutaki, the second-most-visited island, testing the tourism economy.
COVID-19 closed borders for nearly two years, collapsing tourism; borders reopened in May 2022.
February: signed a comprehensive strategic partnership with China, straining relations with New Zealand.

outlook_next_decade: Tourism has recovered and seabed-minerals exploration (manganese nodules) offers a possible second pillar, though commercial mining remains uncertain and environmentally contested. The 2025 China partnership signals a more contested geopolitical position between Wellington and Beijing. The base case is tourism-led growth with the familiar cyclone and pandemic tail risks.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
